04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

After the meeting with Helen Ward, Emma kept returning to the distinction that had shaped the investigation: a selection decision was not a completed payment. The copy Helen had shown her named a successful application, subject to confirmation of enrolment and travel costs. Yet Emma had neither authenticated the copy nor established whether the conditions were met.

The following morning Helen wrote that her cousin would allow a redacted scan to be examined privately by the newsroom. Names, addresses and course details were concealed; publication was not authorised. Emma acknowledged the restrictions before receiving the file and stored it in a limited-access folder.

She compared its formatting with the blank notice previously supplied by Fiona Bell. The headings and the paragraph about reviews appeared consistent. That gave her a useful point of comparison, not independent authentication: a convincing reproduction could still be incomplete or altered.

Sarah pointed to the final line. “Payment subject to final verification.”

“Which means this isn't a receipt,” Emma said.

Nor did the document contain a completed transfer date. Emma asked Helen whether her cousin possessed an account statement or subsequent notice showing that money had arrived. Helen did not know and would enquire without committing her cousin to further contact.

Fiona's latest update introduced another kind of record. The trust's team had identified a list of payment authorisations, although it remained incompletely catalogued and was not available to Emma. Fiona stressed that approving a payment was an administrative step distinct from executing a bank transfer. Individual records might also contain protected personal information.

The phrase brought Emma back to the anonymous telephone warning: ask who approved the payments. She had no evidence that the caller knew the answer or had acted in good faith. Still, the existence of an authorisation list made the question testable.

She divided her notebook into Selected, Authorised and Transferred. Each stage would require separate documentary support. She would not treat a mismatch as evidence of wrongdoing without checking explanations such as withdrawn courses, delayed paperwork or different accounting dates.

Sarah wondered whether Helen's cousin might appear in the payment records. Emma would not try to identify a private student through Fiona's files. If Helen's cousin chose to provide evidence of a transfer, the newsroom could compare the dates and descriptions without publishing personal details.

That evening another message arrived from Fiona. The records inventory included a separate heading, “Payment exceptions — 2011”. The team had not inspected the documents beneath it.

“Exceptions,” Sarah repeated when Emma told her. “That sounds suspicious.”

“It may refer to routine delays or corrections,” Emma said. “We need to know what the trust meant by the word.”

The new label did not prove that money was missing. It did, however, bring the investigation back to the boundary between approval and payment—and to a question the anonymous caller had raised before Emma had the evidence to understand it.
